semantic_correction.stem: A client with cirrhosis and esophageal varices has never had a variceal hemorrhage. Which teaching is most accurate about reducing the risk of a first bleed?

options.A: Follow the prescribed primary-prophylaxis plan, which may use a nonselective beta blocker or endoscopic ligation when appropriate, and seek urgent care for bleeding signs.
options.B: Rely mainly on avoiding coughing or straining because portal-pressure treatment is not important before a first hemorrhage.
options.C: Begin daily aspirin to protect the varices because antiplatelet therapy reduces the chance of rupture.
options.D: Wait until a first hemorrhage occurs before starting preventive treatment because pre-bleed therapy adds little benefit.

semantic_correction.rationale: Current AASLD practice guidance supports primary prevention of variceal hemorrhage before a first bleed. Nonselective beta blockers are central portal-pressure-directed therapy in appropriate patients with clinically significant portal hypertension, and endoscopic variceal ligation is an established primary-prophylaxis option in appropriate esophageal-varix settings, including when beta blockers are not suitable. Prevention should therefore follow the individualized hepatology plan rather than unproven behavioral rules. Hematemesis or melena can represent acute gastrointestinal or variceal bleeding and requires urgent evaluation. Aspirin is not routinely started to prevent variceal rupture. Therefore option A is the most accurate teaching.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach that prevention of first esophageal-variceal hemorrhage uses evidence-based portal-pressure or endoscopic prophylaxis when indicated, with urgent evaluation for bleeding signs.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests evidence-based primary prophylaxis without prescribing the same modality to every client or relying on unsupported cough/strain avoidance.

option_audit.A: Correct. It reflects evidence-based primary prophylaxis and appropriate escalation for bleeding signs.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Avoiding coughing or straining is not a substitute for indicated portal-pressure or endoscopic prophylaxis.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Aspirin is not routine primary prophylaxis for variceal rupture and can increase bleeding risk in some contexts.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Primary prophylaxis is specifically used before a first hemorrhage in appropriate patients.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone reflects current AASLD primary-prevention principles while preserving individualized treatment selection.
cueing_check: All four choices are prevention-teaching statements of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
